title: Following value through a supply chain
prompt: A domestic farm sells grain to a domestic mill for $40. The mill sells flour to a domestic bakery for $70. The bakery sells bread to households for $100. All production occurs this year, with no imported inputs or inventories. What total value does this chain add to GDP?
explanation: The farm adds $40, the mill adds $30 and the bakery adds $30. Adding value added gives $100, equal to the final bread sale; adding all sales would count intermediate products repeatedly.
hint: Subtract purchased intermediate inputs at each production stage.
skill: following value through a supply chain

title: An imported component in a domestic product
prompt: A domestic bicycle maker imports a frame for $200, adds domestic labor and other domestic value worth $300, and sells the finished bicycle to a household for $500. With no other inputs, how much does this transaction chain add to domestic GDP?
explanation: The household purchase is $500, but $200 reflects production abroad and is subtracted as an import. Domestic value added is $300.
hint: Separate the bicycle’s final sale price from the part produced abroad.
skill: an imported component in a domestic product

title: Construction versus a change of ownership
prompt: A firm pays $2 million for a newly built domestic warehouse and $3 million for the land beneath it. Ignore brokerage and other current services. What amount represents newly produced fixed investment in GDP?
correct: $2 million.
wrong: $5 million.
$3 million.
Zero because firms do not consume warehouses.
explanation: The warehouse is a newly produced capital good. Existing land changes owners but is not newly produced, so its purchase price is excluded from current production.
hint: Identify what was produced this year rather than merely purchased this year.
skill: construction versus a change of ownership

title: Production at a foreign-owned factory
prompt: A foreign-owned factory produces appliances inside Country A using local workers. How is the factory’s domestic value added treated in Country A’s GDP?
correct: It is included because the production occurs within Country A.
wrong: It is excluded because the owners are foreign.
It is included only if all profits stay in Country A forever.
It is counted only in the owners’ home-country GDP.
explanation: GDP follows production location. Income paid to foreign owners matters for the distinction between domestic production and national income, not for whether this local production enters GDP.
hint: Use the location of production rather than the owner’s nationality.
skill: production at a foreign-owned factory

title: Purchasing shares is not building a factory
prompt: A household buys $5,000 of an existing company’s shares from another household. No intermediary charges a fee. What does this purchase itself add to current GDP?
correct: Nothing; it transfers ownership of an existing financial claim.
wrong: $5,000 of business fixed investment.
$5,000 of household consumption.
$10,000 because both buyer and seller participate.
explanation: National-accounts investment means additions to produced capital and inventories. Trading an existing share reallocates financial ownership without producing a new good or service.
hint: Distinguish financial investment language from production-accounting investment.
skill: purchasing shares is not building a factory

title: Jobs increase while unemployment also rises
prompt: A town has 900 employed residents and 100 unemployed active job seekers. Fifty residents who were outside the labor force start looking; twenty immediately find jobs and thirty do not. Nobody else changes status. What happens to the unemployment rate?
correct: It rises from 10 percent to about 12.38 percent.
wrong: It falls because employment rises to 920.
It stays 10 percent because the original unemployed count is unchanged.
It rises to exactly 15 percent.
explanation: Employment becomes 920, unemployment 130 and the labor force 1,050. The new unemployment rate is 130/1,050≈12.38 percent. Job growth and a rising unemployment rate can coexist when participation increases.
hint: Update both the unemployed count and the labor-force denominator.
skill: jobs increase while unemployment also rises

title: Shorter hours with the same employment count
prompt: A factory keeps all 100 workers employed but cuts each worker’s weekly hours from 40 to 30. What information does an unchanged employment count miss?
correct: Total weekly hours fall by 25 percent.
wrong: Total weekly hours are unchanged because nobody was dismissed.
The unemployment rate must rise by 25 percentage points.
Every worker is now outside the labor force.
explanation: Hours fall from 4,000 to 3,000 while the number employed stays 100. Employment headcounts alone do not measure the full change in labor input or involuntary short hours.
hint: Multiply workers by hours per worker at each date.
skill: shorter hours with the same employment count

title: A transition between jobs
prompt: A nurse leaves a job after moving to another city and actively searches for a position matching her qualifications. The economy is not in recession. Which description best fits this unemployment spell?
correct: Job-search unemployment during a move between suitable positions.
wrong: Unemployment necessarily caused by an economy-wide spending collapse.
Retirement outside the labor force.
Proof that no suitable nursing jobs can ever exist.
explanation: Workers and jobs take time to match, including after relocation. A search spell can occur in an otherwise healthy economy and need not imply a general shortage of demand.
hint: Distinguish the time needed to find a match from a broad fall in economic activity.
skill: a transition between jobs

title: Real GDP per person and the typical household
prompt: Real GDP per person rises, but most of the additional income goes to a small group and pollution worsens. What can the GDP figure alone establish?
correct: Average measured production per person rose; it does not establish that most households became better off.
wrong: Every resident’s income rose by the same percentage.
Pollution damage is fully deducted from GDP by definition.
The typical household’s welfare must have fallen by exactly the GDP increase.
explanation: GDP per person is an average production measure. Distribution, environmental conditions and other aspects of living standards require additional evidence.
hint: Ask which outcomes the aggregate average directly measures.
skill: real gdp per person and the typical household

title: Stocks and flows in a city report
prompt: A city reports debt of $80 million on December 31 and a budget deficit of $5 million during that year. Why are these different types of measures?
correct: Debt is an amount outstanding at a date; the deficit is borrowing needs measured over a period.
wrong: Both are annual flows and can be compared as if they covered identical periods.
Debt is the city’s annual spending and the deficit is its population.
A positive deficit means the debt stock must be zero.
explanation: A stock records an accumulated position at one moment; a flow records activity during an interval. Comparing or combining them requires consistent dates and any relevant adjustments.
hint: Look for an as-of date versus a during-the-year interval.
skill: stocks and flows in a city report

title: Two households face different price pressures
prompt: Rent rises 10 percent and all other prices are unchanged. Household A originally spent half its budget on rent; household B spent one-quarter. Holding each household’s purchased quantities fixed, whose total cost rises more in percentage terms?
correct: A’s cost rises 5 percent and B’s rises 2.5 percent.
wrong: Both costs rise 10 percent because rent inflation is the same.
A’s cost rises 2.5 percent and B’s rises 5 percent.
Neither household is affected unless every price rises.
explanation: A category’s contribution depends on its initial spending share. Multiplying the 10 percent rent increase by shares of one-half and one-quarter gives 5 and 2.5 percent.
hint: Weight the price increase by each household’s original rent share.
skill: two households face different price pressures

title: Slower inflation is not lower prices
prompt: A price index rises from 100 to 108 in one year and then to 112.32 the next. Which description is correct?
correct: Prices are still rising, but inflation slows from 8 percent to 4 percent.
wrong: The price level falls in the second year.
Inflation rises from 8 percent to 12.32 percent in the second year.
Prices return to their initial level because inflation slows.
explanation: The second-year increase is 4.32/108=4 percent. A lower positive inflation rate means the price level increases more slowly, not that earlier price increases are reversed.
hint: Calculate each year’s percentage change using that year’s starting index.
skill: slower inflation is not lower prices

title: A pay raise and purchasing power
prompt: A worker’s annual pay rises from $40,000 to $42,000 while the price of her unchanged consumption basket rises 8 percent. What happens to her purchasing power?
correct: It falls by about 2.78 percent.
wrong: It rises 5 percent because her paycheck is larger.
It falls exactly 8 percent.
It is unchanged because both pay and prices rise.
explanation: Pay rises by a factor of 1.05 while the basket costs 1.08 times as much. Purchasing power changes by 1.05/1.08−1≈−2.78 percent.
hint: Compare the pay growth factor with the basket-price growth factor.
skill: a pay raise and purchasing power

title: One price rises faster than the rest
prompt: A meal’s price rises from $10 to $12 while the overall price level rises 10 percent. Has the meal become more expensive relative to other goods on average?
correct: Yes; its relative price rises by about 9.09 percent.
wrong: No; any inflation leaves every relative price unchanged.
Yes; its relative price rises exactly 20 percent.
No; its relative price falls by 10 percent.
explanation: The meal’s price factor is 1.20 and the general price factor is 1.10. The ratio 1.20/1.10≈1.0909 shows a relative increase of about 9.09 percent.
hint: Remove the overall price change before interpreting the specific price increase.
skill: one price rises faster than the rest

title: An indexed benefit with a different personal basket
prompt: A monthly benefit rises 4 percent because it is indexed to a broad price measure. A recipient’s own fixed basket becomes 7 percent more expensive. What follows for the benefit’s purchasing power over that basket?
correct: It falls despite the nominal increase.
wrong: It is fully protected against every recipient’s personal cost increase.
It rises by exactly 3 percent.
It falls only if the nominal benefit is cut.
explanation: Indexation protects against the chosen index, not every household-specific price pattern. Here the payment factor 1.04 is smaller than the basket-cost factor 1.07.
hint: Compare the index used for adjustment with the prices the recipient actually faces.
skill: an indexed benefit with a different personal basket

title: A fixed cash budget buys fewer baskets
prompt: A club has an unchanged $1,200 budget. A standard supply bundle rises in price from $40 to $50. How many fewer whole bundles can it buy if it spends the entire budget on these bundles?
correct: 6 fewer bundles.
wrong: 10 fewer bundles.
5 fewer bundles.
30 fewer bundles.
explanation: The club could buy 1,200/40=30 bundles and can now buy 1,200/50=24. The loss is six bundles; an unchanged nominal budget need not maintain real purchasing capacity.
hint: Divide the budget by each price before taking the difference.
skill: a fixed cash budget buys fewer baskets

title: Deflation and the value of cash
prompt: A person holds $100 in cash for a year and earns no interest. The price of an unchanged basket falls from $20 to $16. How many baskets can the cash buy at the end compared with the start?
correct: 6.25 rather than 5 baskets.
wrong: 4 rather than 5 baskets.
5 baskets at both dates.
20 rather than 16 baskets.
explanation: The cash amount is unchanged, but dividing by the lower price gives 100/16=6.25 instead of 100/20=5. Falling prices raise its purchasing power over this basket.
hint: Keep the dollar amount fixed and change only the basket price.
skill: deflation and the value of cash

title: Sales revenue grows without more production
prompt: A small economy produces only 100 identical tables in each of two years. Their price rises from $50 to $55. What changes?
correct: Nominal GDP rises 10 percent, while real output is unchanged.
wrong: Real output rises 10 percent because sales revenue rises.
Both nominal and real GDP fall.
Nominal GDP is unchanged because quantities are fixed.
explanation: Revenue rises from $5,000 to $5,500 entirely because of price. Valuing both years at the same table price leaves real production equal.
hint: Separate the quantity produced from the price used to value it.
skill: sales revenue grows without more production

title: Price indexes with different reference years
prompt: Two reports show price indexes of 120 and 150, but each uses a different reference year equal to 100. Can these index numbers alone establish which economy has the higher cost of living?
correct: No; differently normalized indexes do not directly compare price levels across economies.
wrong: Yes; 150 always means living costs are 25 percent higher than where the index is 120.
Yes; the economy with 120 has experienced no inflation.
No price index can ever measure changes over time.
explanation: An index’s level depends on its reference normalization and basket. It can track changes within a consistent series, but comparing living costs requires comparable goods and units.
hint: Check whether the two index scales and baskets are comparable.
skill: price indexes with different reference years

title: A better product and measured inflation
prompt: A new refrigerator costs more than the old model but also uses less electricity and has more storage. Why might a price statistician adjust for quality before treating the entire sticker-price increase as inflation?
correct: Part of the higher price may pay for a different amount or quality of service.
wrong: Every more expensive new product must have a lower quality-adjusted price.
Quality improvements make the purchase disappear from household spending.
Inflation measures are defined to ignore all durable goods.
explanation: A like-for-like price comparison tries to distinguish a higher price for the same service from paying for a changed product. The direction and size of a quality adjustment require evidence, not an automatic rule.
hint: Ask whether the two sticker prices refer to an equivalent product.
skill: a better product and measured inflation

title: A larger economy with less output per person
prompt: Over a decade, real GDP rises 10 percent while population rises 20 percent. What happens to real GDP per person?
correct: It falls by about 8.33 percent.
wrong: It rises 10 percent because total GDP rises.
It falls exactly 10 percent.
It rises 30 percent.
explanation: Output per person changes by the ratio 1.10/1.20≈0.9167. Total production can grow while production per resident falls if population grows faster.
hint: Divide the output growth factor by the population growth factor.
skill: a larger economy with less output per person

title: Replacing worn-out equipment
prompt: A workshop begins the year with 50 identical machines. Five wear out completely, and it purchases seven new machines. There are no other capital changes. How much does its machine stock grow?
correct: By 2 machines.
wrong: By 7 machines.
By 12 machines.
It falls by 5 machines.
explanation: Gross investment adds seven machines, but depreciation removes five. Net investment is two, leaving 52 machines at the end of the year.
hint: Subtract worn-out capital from new capital before computing the net addition.
skill: replacing worn-out equipment

title: Equipment without the missing skills
prompt: A firm installs advanced equipment, but workers have not been trained to operate it. Why might a training program raise the return from that equipment?
correct: Worker skills and equipment can be complementary inputs.
wrong: Training necessarily makes physical capital unnecessary.
The purchase price of equipment fixes its productivity regardless of use.
Human capital means only the number of people employed.
explanation: Skills can make existing equipment usable or more effective. Productive capacity depends on how inputs work together, not merely on the amount spent on machinery.
hint: Identify the missing input needed to use the installed equipment effectively.
skill: equipment without the missing skills

title: Long-run compounding changes a comparison
prompt: Two economies start with the same real income per person. One grows 2 percent annually and the other 3 percent for many years. Which statement follows if those rates persist?
correct: The 3 percent economy’s relative income advantage grows over time.
wrong: The difference remains exactly one percent of the initial income forever.
Their incomes must become equal again after ten years.
A one-percentage-point growth difference has no long-run effect.
explanation: Each year the faster-growing economy multiplies its income by a larger factor. Repeated multiplication makes the relative gap grow, even though the growth-rate difference is only one percentage point.
hint: Compare repeated growth factors rather than adding the rates once.
skill: long-run compounding changes a comparison

title: More output from a better schedule
prompt: A delivery company uses the same vehicles, fuel and worker hours but adopts routing software that allows more deliveries. What is the most direct description of the improvement?
correct: Higher productivity from using existing inputs more effectively.
wrong: Output growth caused entirely by more hours worked.
Capital depreciation becoming negative by definition.
A rise in inflation rather than a change in productive performance.
explanation: Producing more service with the same measured inputs indicates improved efficiency or technology. It differs from increasing output simply by supplying more inputs.
hint: Check whether input quantities changed along with output.
skill: more output from a better schedule

title: Building capacity uses resources today
prompt: An economy at full use of its current resources redirects workers and materials from household goods to constructing water infrastructure. What immediate tradeoff is possible?
correct: Fewer household goods now in exchange for infrastructure that may support future production.
wrong: More of every good now with no resource tradeoff under the stated full-use assumption.
No future benefit is possible from public capital.
The infrastructure is free because government purchases it.
explanation: At full resource use, more production of one category generally requires less of another. Infrastructure may raise future capacity, but financing does not remove today’s real resource cost.
hint: Distinguish the future benefit from the current resources needed to build it.
skill: building capacity uses resources today

title: Saving is useful only with productive allocation
prompt: Two countries devote the same share of income to new capital. One builds well-used equipment; the other builds facilities that remain idle because they lack connections to users. Why need their growth gains differ?
correct: The productivity and use of investment matter, not just its spending share.
wrong: Equal investment spending guarantees equal future output.
Unused capital always has the highest return.
Growth depends only on how many dollars were recorded as investment.
explanation: Investment is a resource commitment rather than a guarantee of productive services. Complementary infrastructure, maintenance and allocation can determine whether capital raises output.
hint: Ask what services the completed investment actually provides.
skill: saving is useful only with productive allocation

title: An idea that several producers can use
prompt: A new production technique can be used by many firms at once without being used up. Why can its benefits extend beyond the inventor?
correct: Knowledge can spread and improve other firms’ production without exhausting the original idea.
wrong: The inventor must lose the ability to use it whenever another firm learns it.
Creating any idea uses no resources.
Every useful idea must be available to everyone without legal restrictions.
explanation: Ideas can be nonrival even when discovery is costly and access is restricted. Diffusion and spillovers help explain why research benefits need not be confined to the original developer.
hint: Separate the cost of discovering an idea from the cost of another person using it.
skill: an idea that several producers can use

title: Predictable rules and a long-lived project
prompt: A business can build a plant that pays off over twenty years. Investors become less confident that contracts will be enforced, while the plant’s engineering performance is unchanged. How can this affect investment?
correct: The expected ability to receive future returns falls, making some projects less attractive.
wrong: Engineering productivity alone determines every investment decision.
Weaker contract enforcement necessarily lowers the project’s construction cost to zero.
Investors must build more plants whenever uncertainty rises.
explanation: Investment depends on both productive returns and whether those returns can be retained. Institutional predictability can affect incentives without changing the physical production technique.
hint: Consider the difference between producing revenue and being able to collect it.
skill: predictable rules and a long-lived project

title: A temporary boom is not proof of faster trend growth
prompt: Restaurants reopen unused dining rooms after a short disruption and output rebounds rapidly for several months. What additional evidence is needed before calling this a permanent increase in the economy’s growth rate?
correct: Evidence of sustained expansion in productive capacity or productivity, beyond restoring previously idle activity.
wrong: None; any rapid rebound must continue at the same rate forever.
A higher price for meals alone proves faster real growth.
A return to normal opening hours permanently changes the population growth rate.
explanation: A rebound can reflect recovery toward an existing capacity level. Maintaining unusually rapid growth after that recovery requires additional sources of capacity or productivity growth.
hint: Separate catching back up to an earlier level from raising the long-run growth path.
skill: a temporary boom is not proof of faster trend growth

title: Unexpected shelves of unsold goods
prompt: A retailer plans to sell 100 units this week, receives 100 units, but sells only 70. If it wants to keep its normal inventory target and expects weak sales to continue, what is a likely next adjustment?
correct: Reduce future orders, transmitting weaker sales to its suppliers.
wrong: Increase orders solely because unsold inventory rose.
Treat the unsold 30 units as proof that customer demand increased.
Assume the inventory surprise has no possible effect on production decisions.
explanation: Unexpected inventory accumulation signals that demand fell short of plans. Reducing orders helps return stocks toward the desired level and can lower upstream production.
hint: Compare actual sales with the purchases made in anticipation of sales.
skill: unexpected shelves of unsold goods

title: Everyone tries to save more during a slump
prompt: In a stylized closed economy with idle capacity, fixed prices and unchanged planned investment and government purchases, households cut consumption to save more. What can happen to total income?
correct: It falls as businesses respond to weaker demand, so intended saving need not become an equally large increase in realized saving.
wrong: It must rise immediately because all saving creates equal new orders automatically.
It is fixed by definition regardless of production and employment.
Every household’s income is guaranteed to remain unchanged.
explanation: One household can save by reducing spending, but when many do so together, other households and firms lose sales and income. The stated model does not assume investment rises to offset the consumption decline.
hint: Track how one person’s spending becomes another person’s income.
skill: everyone tries to save more during a slump

title: Investment responds to expected customers
prompt: A manufacturer can borrow cheaply but expects weak demand and already has idle machines. Why might a lower borrowing rate fail to trigger much new equipment spending?
correct: Expected sales and existing capacity also influence the payoff from investment.
wrong: Borrowing cost is the only determinant of investment under every circumstance.
Idle machines count as negative physical capital.
A lower interest rate legally requires firms to invest.
explanation: Cheaper finance helps only if an additional project is sufficiently attractive. Weak expected sales can leave the expected benefit below even a reduced financing cost.
hint: Compare the expected use of new capacity with its cost.
skill: investment responds to expected customers

title: Three rounds of a spending expansion
prompt: In a simple fixed-price economy, an initial $100 purchase becomes income. Recipients spend 60 percent of each additional dollar on domestic output, which becomes someone else’s income. Ignoring taxes, imports and all later rounds, what is total spending in the initial round and the next two rounds?
explanation: The three rounds are $100, $60 and $36. Adding them gives $196; the infinite-round multiplier would answer a different question.
hint: List the three specified rounds before adding them.
skill: three rounds of a spending expansion

title: The first round of a transfer versus a purchase
prompt: A government can either buy $100 of newly produced domestic services or transfer $100 to households, which initially spend 80 percent of extra disposable income on domestic goods. Other behavior is held fixed. Which creates more direct first-round demand for current domestic output?
correct: The purchase creates $100; the transfer initially creates $80.
wrong: Both create exactly $100 of first-round demand under the stated spending behavior.
The transfer creates $180 while the purchase creates zero.
Neither can affect demand because both are government actions.
explanation: Government purchases directly buy output. A transfer raises household resources, but the stated household behavior spends only $80 initially; later effects are outside this first-round comparison.
hint: Distinguish a payment for current output from a transfer that may subsequently be spent.
skill: the first round of a transfer versus a purchase

title: Two shocks pull output in opposite directions
prompt: In the short-run AD-AS model, household spending rises while a disruption also raises firms’ production costs. What can be said without knowing which shock is larger?
correct: Both push the price level up, but their effects on output oppose each other.
wrong: Both necessarily raise output.
Both necessarily lower the price level.
Output and prices must remain unchanged because there are two shocks.
explanation: Higher demand tends to raise output and prices. A reduction in short-run supply tends to lower output and raise prices. The output result depends on their relative magnitudes.
hint: Analyze each shift separately before combining its price and output effects.
skill: two shocks pull output in opposite directions

title: A family uses savings after a temporary income loss
prompt: A household expects a one-month interruption in earnings and has enough liquid savings to cover normal expenses. Why might its spending fall less than its current income?
correct: It can draw down savings to smooth purchases across the temporary interruption.
wrong: Spending must always equal income in each month.
Using savings creates new labor income automatically.
The interruption raises the household’s lifetime resources.
explanation: Financial buffers allow a household to separate the timing of spending from the timing of income. Expectations and access to savings matter; a prolonged loss or limited liquidity could produce a different response.
hint: Include the household’s existing assets as well as this month’s paycheck.
skill: a family uses savings after a temporary income loss

title: A stimulus project arrives after conditions change
prompt: A public construction project was proposed during a downturn but begins after demand has recovered and builders are fully booked. Why can its short-run effect differ from the original forecast?
correct: The project now competes more directly for scarce workers and materials than when capacity was idle.
wrong: Implementation timing never changes economic effects.
Any project approved during a recession creates idle resources forever.
Full booking guarantees the project has zero cost.
explanation: The same spending can meet unused capacity in one period and bid resources away from other uses in another. Delays change the conditions under which the spending occurs.
hint: Evaluate resource availability when spending happens, not only when it was proposed.
skill: a stimulus project arrives after conditions change

title: A budget surplus does not reveal the policy change
prompt: Tax revenue rises strongly as employment and incomes recover, while tax rules and spending commitments are unchanged. Why does the improved budget balance not by itself prove a new austerity policy?
correct: Economic recovery can improve the balance under unchanged policy rules.
wrong: Every improvement in the balance requires a newly passed tax increase.
Employment cannot affect tax revenue.
A budget balance measures only changes in laws, not actual receipts and payments.
explanation: Budget outcomes reflect both policy settings and the state of the economy. Identifying a discretionary change requires comparing rules and decisions, not just the observed balance.
hint: Separate changes in the tax base from changes in tax policy.
skill: a budget surplus does not reveal the policy change

title: A closure in one industry and the whole economy
prompt: A declining industry loses 10,000 jobs while expanding industries add 15,000 over the same period. What does this establish about total employment across these industries?
correct: It rises by 5,000, even though the declining industry’s workers may face serious adjustment costs.
wrong: It falls by 10,000 because closures are more visible.
Every displaced worker necessarily found one of the new jobs.
The economy must be in a recession because one industry contracted.
explanation: The aggregate net change is 15,000−10,000=5,000. That arithmetic does not show that the same people moved smoothly between jobs or that their earnings were preserved.
hint: Separate the net count from who bears the transition costs.
skill: a closure in one industry and the whole economy

title: A loan creates two balance-sheet entries
prompt: A bank grants a customer a $10,000 loan and credits that amount to the customer’s deposit account at the same bank. At origination, before any spending or fees, how do the bank’s assets and liabilities change?
correct: Loan assets and deposit liabilities each rise by $10,000.
wrong: Only the bank’s equity rises by $10,000.
Deposits fall by $10,000 while loans rise.
The bank obtains a $10,000 profit immediately.
explanation: The bank acquires a claim on the borrower and owes an equal deposit balance. Creating a loan does not create equal equity or eliminate credit, funding and regulatory constraints.
hint: Record what the customer owes the bank and what the bank owes the customer.
skill: a loan creates two balance-sheet entries

title: A payment between two banks
prompt: A customer at Bank A pays $500 to a seller at Bank B. The banks settle the payment by transferring central-bank reserve balances. Ignoring fees, what happens to reserves in the banking system as a whole?
correct: Their total is unchanged; $500 moves from A to B.
wrong: Their total falls by $500 because the customer spent money.
Their total rises by $500 because the seller received a deposit.
Every bank’s reserve balance rises by $500.
explanation: Settlement reallocates existing reserve balances between banks. One bank’s reserve loss is the other bank’s gain, separate from any central-bank action changing aggregate reserves.
hint: Add the reserve changes at both banks.
skill: a payment between two banks

title: Loan losses and the equity cushion
prompt: A bank has assets of $120 million and liabilities of $110 million. It writes off $6 million of unrecoverable loans, with liabilities and all other asset values unchanged. What equity remains?
correct: $4 million.
wrong: $10 million.
$16 million.
$104 million.
explanation: Initial equity is 120−110=10. The loan loss reduces assets to 114 and equity to 114−110=4; creditors’ claims do not fall merely because the asset was written off.
hint: Recompute assets minus liabilities after the loss.
skill: loan losses and the equity cushion

title: A liquid asset shortage is not the same as insolvency
prompt: A bank owns assets worth more than its liabilities but cannot immediately sell its long-term loans at their normal value to meet a sudden withdrawal. What problem does this description directly identify?
correct: A liquidity shortage, which is distinct from having liabilities exceed asset value.
wrong: Insolvency by definition, regardless of asset values.
A guaranteed profit with no risk.
A lack of deposits that can never be addressed by borrowing or asset sales.
explanation: The bank may have positive net worth yet lack immediately available means of payment. Whether emergency funding helps depends on asset quality and other conditions, but timing and net worth are different questions.
hint: Compare the timing of payments with the value of assets and liabilities.
skill: a liquid asset shortage is not the same as insolvency

title: Repaying a bank loan with a deposit
prompt: A borrower repays $1,000 of loan principal using a deposit at the same bank. Ignore interest, fees and every other transaction. What happens on the bank’s balance sheet?
correct: The loan asset and deposit liability both fall by $1,000.
wrong: The loan asset rises while the deposit liability falls.
The bank’s equity rises by $1,000 automatically.
Both the loan and deposit remain unchanged because money only changes owners.
explanation: The borrower’s deposit claim and debt to the bank are reduced together. Principal repayment is not bank profit; interest and fees would require separate entries.
hint: Reverse the principal amount of the original loan-and-deposit entries.
skill: repaying a bank loan with a deposit

title: Policy rates and customer borrowing rates
prompt: A central bank cuts its policy rate, but a borrower’s credit risk rises sharply. Why might that borrower’s loan rate not fall?
correct: The lender’s risk premium can rise enough to offset the lower policy-related funding rate.
wrong: Every private loan rate must equal the policy rate exactly.
Borrower risk affects only loans made by governments.
A policy-rate cut automatically cancels existing defaults.
explanation: Customer rates incorporate credit risk, funding, maturity and other factors. Monetary easing can reduce one component without forcing the total rate lower for every borrower.
hint: Break the customer rate into the common rate component and the borrower-specific spread.
skill: policy rates and customer borrowing rates

title: Fixed versus adjustable mortgage payments
prompt: Two households have otherwise comparable mortgages. One has a fixed payment contract; the other resets its interest rate next month. Market rates rise. Which household is more directly exposed to an immediate payment increase through its existing contract?
correct: The household whose rate resets next month.
wrong: The fixed-payment household, because fixed means automatically adjusted.
Both existing contracts must change payments identically next month.
Neither can be affected by interest rates under any contract.
explanation: Resetting passes current rates into required payments more quickly. Fixed contracts can still be affected when refinancing or through other economic channels, but their existing payment terms do not immediately reset.
hint: Check when each contract updates its rate.
skill: fixed versus adjustable mortgage payments

title: More reserves do not force more lending
prompt: A bank receives additional central-bank reserves but sees few creditworthy applicants and wants to preserve its equity cushion. What follows?
correct: It need not expand lending by a fixed multiple of the added reserves.
wrong: It must lend a predetermined multiple regardless of borrowers, capital and risk.
Reserves and bank equity are identical, so every constraint disappears.
A reserve increase gives the bank ownership of every borrower’s income.
explanation: Loan decisions depend on expected returns, credit risk, capital, funding and regulation. A mechanical reserve multiplier is not a universal description of bank lending.
hint: Identify the constraints and incentives beyond the quantity of reserve assets.
skill: more reserves do not force more lending

title: A price target and an inflation-rate target
prompt: A central bank seeks 2 percent annual inflation rather than a return to a fixed past price level. If inflation returns to 2 percent after a year of unusually high inflation, what normally follows from the rate target alone?
correct: The price level continues rising at 2 percent rather than automatically returning to its earlier level.
wrong: Every earlier price increase must be reversed.
The price level becomes constant because the target is met.
All individual prices must rise exactly 2 percent.
explanation: An inflation-rate target describes the pace of change in a broad price index. It does not, by itself, require making up past misses or controlling every price separately.
hint: Distinguish the target for a growth rate from a target for an index level.
skill: a price target and an inflation-rate target

title: Stabilization after an energy disruption
prompt: An energy shortage raises production costs and reduces output in a standard short-run demand-and-supply model. Why can monetary policymakers face a difficult tradeoff?
correct: Reducing demand can restrain price pressure but may further weaken output in the short run.
wrong: A single demand contraction must simultaneously raise output and lower all prices.
Monetary policy directly creates the missing physical energy supply.
The shortage has no possible effect on inflation.
explanation: A supply disruption moves prices and output in unfavorable directions. A demand-management tool does not directly repair the supply loss, so stabilizing one objective can worsen another in the short run.
hint: Separate a supply repair from changing total spending.
skill: stabilization after an energy disruption

title: Travel becomes more expensive in home currency
prompt: A traveler earns home currency and plans a trip priced in foreign currency. One foreign unit initially costs 2 home units and later costs 2.5 home units, while foreign hotel prices are unchanged. What happens to the trip’s home-currency cost?
correct: It rises 25 percent.
wrong: It falls 25 percent.
It rises 0.5 percent.
It stays unchanged because hotel prices abroad did not change.
explanation: Each foreign unit now requires 2.5/2=1.25 times as much home currency. The traveler’s cost rises even when the hotel’s foreign-currency price is fixed.
hint: Compare the home-currency price of one foreign unit before and after.
skill: travel becomes more expensive in home currency

title: An exporter’s margin depends on the invoice currency
prompt: A domestic producer sells an item for a fixed invoice of 100 foreign currency units and incurs domestic costs of 60 home units. One foreign unit rises in value from 0.8 to 1 home unit before payment; quantities and costs stay fixed. What happens to the producer’s home-currency margin?
correct: It rises from 20 to 40 home units.
wrong: It falls from 40 to 20 home units.
It stays 40 home units.
It rises from 60 to 100 home units.
explanation: Revenue rises from 100×0.8=80 to 100×1=100 home units. Subtracting the unchanged cost of 60 gives margins of 20 and 40. Invoice currency matters for who initially bears exchange-rate changes.
hint: Convert revenue into the same currency as costs before subtracting.
skill: an exporter’s margin depends on the invoice currency

title: Why imports are subtracted in GDP accounting
prompt: A household purchases an imported laptop for $900. Ignoring domestic retail services, why does subtracting imports from expenditure GDP not mean imports mechanically destroy $900 of domestic production?
correct: The subtraction removes foreign production already included in the household’s $900 consumption purchase.
wrong: Imported goods are excluded from consumption spending altogether.
Every imported laptop necessarily eliminates exactly $900 of domestic output.
Imports are subtracted because they have no value to households.
explanation: The consumption entry includes the purchase, and the import entry removes its foreign-produced content. This avoids counting foreign output as domestic GDP; the behavioral effect on domestic production is a separate question.
hint: Trace both expenditure entries generated by the same imported purchase.
skill: why imports are subtracted in gdp accounting

title: A trade deficit is not a government deficit
prompt: A country imports more goods and services than it exports, while its government budget is balanced. Is this combination possible?
correct: Yes; the trade balance and government budget describe different transactions.
wrong: No; a trade deficit is defined as government spending minus tax revenue.
No; a balanced government budget requires every private firm to export.
Yes, but only if all imports are free gifts.
explanation: The trade balance concerns exports and imports. The fiscal balance concerns government receipts and payments; private saving and investment also affect external balances.
hint: Identify the actors and transactions included in each balance.
skill: a trade deficit is not a government deficit

title: Foreign finance and a domestic construction project
prompt: A foreign investor pays for construction of a new factory inside the domestic economy, using domestic construction labor and materials. Which statement is correct?
correct: The domestic construction adds to domestic investment and GDP, even though finance comes from abroad.
wrong: Foreign finance automatically excludes the factory from domestic GDP.
The project adds only to exports because the owner is foreign.
Financing and construction are the same entry and should be counted twice.
explanation: GDP tracks production within the economy. The financing transaction explains who supplies funds and receives ownership claims; it is distinct from the factory’s production.
hint: Separate where the funds originate from where construction occurs.
skill: foreign finance and a domestic construction project

title: A foreign downturn reaches domestic producers
prompt: A country’s major trading partners enter a recession and reduce purchases from its exporters. In a short-run model with idle capacity and no offsetting changes, what is the likely domestic effect?
correct: Lower export demand reduces sales and can lower domestic production and employment.
wrong: Domestic demand must rise by exactly the export loss automatically.
Foreign spending never affects domestic output.
The shock necessarily improves every domestic firm’s sales.
explanation: Exports are part of demand for domestic output. A foreign recession can therefore transmit weaker spending to domestic firms, even without an initial domestic policy change.
hint: Follow the reduction in customers’ orders across the border.
skill: a foreign downturn reaches domestic producers

title: An import leakage in a spending round
prompt: A household receives $100 of additional income and spends $70. Of that spending, $20 buys imported goods with no domestic value added. How much direct additional demand for domestic output comes from this household’s spending round?
explanation: Domestic purchases are total spending of $70 less imported spending of $20, leaving $50. The $30 saved is a different leakage from current consumption.
hint: Separate the portion saved from the portion spent on foreign production.
skill: an import leakage in a spending round

title: A weaker currency and higher domestic prices
prompt: A domestic product’s home-currency price rises 20 percent while the value of one home currency unit falls from 1 to 0.9 foreign currency units. What happens to the product’s foreign-currency price if both changes fully apply?
correct: It rises 8 percent.
wrong: It falls 10 percent.
It falls 8 percent.
It remains unchanged.
explanation: The foreign-currency price factor is 1.20×0.90=1.08. Domestic price increases can more than offset the apparent price advantage of a weaker currency.
hint: Combine the product-price change with the currency-conversion change.
skill: a weaker currency and higher domestic prices

title: A promised fixed exchange rate faces selling pressure
prompt: A central bank promises a fixed home-currency price of foreign currency and offers to trade at that rate. Private demand for foreign currency exceeds private supply. To meet the excess demand at the promised rate, what transaction is needed if no other adjustment occurs?
correct: The central bank sells foreign reserves and receives home currency.
wrong: The central bank buys additional foreign reserves using home currency.
Every foreign seller must reduce its prices by law.
The exchange rate floats freely without any change to the promise.
explanation: Maintaining the quoted price requires supplying the foreign currency the market lacks. Reserve availability and other policy choices constrain how long this can continue.
hint: Determine which currency is in excess demand and who must supply it.
skill: a promised fixed exchange rate faces selling pressure

title: Can every country run a trade surplus?
prompt: In a fully recorded world where every cross-border goods-and-services sale is measured consistently, could every country have exports greater than imports at the same time?
correct: No; one country’s export is another country’s import, so world net exports sum to zero.
wrong: Yes; every country can export without another country importing.
Yes; larger populations eliminate the accounting link.
No; international trade requires every individual country to have exactly balanced trade.
explanation: Individual countries can have surpluses or deficits, but those balances offset globally under consistent measurement. The identity does not require each country’s own balance to be zero.
hint: Add both sides of each cross-border sale across all countries.
skill: can every country run a trade surplus?
